newsitem.title: USA: Buyers shy away from Apple's Macintosh.
newsitem.headline: Buyers shy away from Apple's Macintosh.

text.p: Technology purchasing managers are having a hard time getting their bosses to approve big orders of Macintosh computers as more doubts swirl around struggling Apple Computer Inc.

Apple, based in Cupertino, Calif., said Friday it expects to report a loss from operations of $100 to $150 million in the December quarter because of weak sales of its consumer machines and a shortage of its popular laptops.
Analysts said the bad financial news puts Apple in a spiral where each time it reports disappointing earnings, more customers shy away, leading to more losses in future quarters.

"It's definitely a fight," said Donald Laird, a computer consultant who advises companies about technology purchases. "Very seldom do I go into a shop where they're as objective (about technology) as I'd like them to be."

The bad news also overshadows Apple's plan to revamp the fundamental software of the Macintosh with help from recently acquired Next Software Inc -- a purchase that could give Apple a clear edge in technology over personal computers running Windows software from Microsoft Corp, Apple customers said.
"It's frustrating," said Jeff Lauterette, technical support engineer at EPI Systems, a big Macintosh dealership based in Rockville, Maryland.
Lots of customers are shying away from Apple, even though the Mac offers better performance in certain applications, Lauterette said.

At a presentation Monday, Apple Chief Technical Officer Ellen Hancock assured big customers that Apple will concentrate on winning back big accounts now that the company has a clear technology strategy.
"We honestly do believe our lack of a (technology) strategy until a couple of weeks ago caused us the problem (with revenue in the December quarter)," Hancock said.
"We are ready to go back on the attack to tell (corporate customers) that we have excellent technology."
Still, Apple will not win new customers with technology alone, Apple buyers said.

"I've been an Apple supporter since early on and the Apple has made a difference in my life," said Don Barrs, a principal at Wilton Manors Elementary school in Florida. "However, I have to be realistic about what's best for our school district and our children."
